analysis.investment_thesis: A micro-cap (INR 69 Cr) commodity plastic pipe maker incorporated in 2017 earning a pitiful 0.26% ROE — that's below a savings account, let alone my 15%+ ROIC threshold. The low P/E of 7.84 is a value trap on near-zero earnings; invert and ask "what could go wrong?" — almost everything already has.
key_strengths: Exposure to India infrastructure/plumbing demand tailwind
key_risks: ROE of 0.26% signals capital destruction, not compounding
Commodity plastic pipes — no moat vs Supreme, Astral, Finolex
Unproven 9-year-old SME with negligible DII (0.07%) validation
red_flags: ROE near zero while carrying invested capital — return profile fails basic quality test
P/E cheapness is illusion: tiny earnings base makes multiple meaningless
No track record through a full cycle; incorporated 2017
analysis.detailed_analysis: Applying inversion: what makes a bad investment? A commodity product, no pricing power, sub-cost-of-capital returns, tiny scale, and no operating history through stress. Malpani Pipes checks every one of those boxes. A 0.26% ROE is a rounding error — capital is being consumed, not compounded. In plastic pipes, the economics belong to scale players with brand (Supreme Industries, Astral, Finolex) who enjoy distribution moats and 18-25% ROCE; a INR 69 Cr upstart has no structural advantage and is a price-taker on PVC resin inputs.\n\nThe 7.84 P/E tempts the naive value investor, but Graham himself warned against cheapness without quality. At this earnings base, one bad quarter of resin volatility wipes out the "E" entirely. High promoter holding of 73.78% is the only positive, but alignment without competence destroys value just as efficiently. I'd rather pay a fair price for Supreme Industries than a cheap price for this. Pass — and as I often say, it's remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid.
